Interstate Transmission System

Supplemental Comments of the Sierra Club 
 
 
Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) October 27, 
2025 Notice Inviting Comments1 on the Department of Energy’s advanced notice of proposed 
rulemaking (“ANOPR”)2 addressing interconnection of large loads to the interstate transmission 
system, the Sierra Club respectfully submits these supplemental comments. As it explained in its 
initial comments, Sierra Club agrees that changes are necessary to incorporate new large loads 
into the transmission system without raising costs and jeopardizing reliability for the hundreds of 
millions of Americans who rely on the grid.3 
 
As detailed in Sierra Club’s previous comments, the rapid proliferation of data centers 
has already caused significant harms to existing ratepayers across the country. Ratepayers in 
PJM, however, have seen an outsized impact. To underscore the need for reforms, 3,844 Sierra 
Club members residing in the PJM footprint signed letters urging the Commission to take action 
that will ensure that costs caused by data center owners are not placed onto Sierra Club members 
and other existing ratepayers.4 Additionally, the Sierra Club chapter directors for all 13 PJM 
states and Washington DC signed a letter urging the Commission to act.5 These letters provide 
 
1 Notice Inviting Comments, Docket No. RM26-4-000 (Oct. 27, 2025). 
2 Secretary of Energy, Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large Loads, 
Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Oct. 23, 2025). 
3 Comments of Public Interest Organizations, Docket No. RM26-4-000 (Nov. 21, 2025). 
4 Attached as Appendix B. 
5 Attached as Appendix A. 

--- PAGE 2 ---
four principles that Sierra Club members and chapter directors believe the Commission should 
use to guide its decision: 
1. The costs to power data centers should be paid for by data center owners, not residential 
ratepayers. 
 
2. FERC should encourage policies to ensure that the lowest-cost energy technologies, 
including abundant, clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal come 
online to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
 
3. State efforts to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, 
should not be undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
 
4. Electric system design should prioritize all consumers, especially small residential 
consumers typically underrepresented in decision-making. 
 
It is not often that thousands of everyday people take the time to make their voices heard 
by the Commission on a complex proceeding like this one. We urge the Commission to consider 
and act on the principles outlined by the 3,812 Sierra Club members and 14 chapter directors as 
it prepares to act on the ANOPR next month. 
May 20, 2026  
 
 
 
 
Respectfully Submitted, 
/s/ Justin Vickers 
Justin Vickers, Senior Attorney

14 May 2026

Attention: Chair Swett, Commissioner Chang, Commissioner See, Commissioner Rosner, and 
Commissioner LaCerte 
 
Dear FERC Commissioners, 
 
We, Directors of the 14 Sierra Club Chapters representing the 13 PJM states and the District of 
Columbia, are committed to ensuring that the region’s energy future is reliable, affordable, and 
aligned with the health and economic well-being of the communities we serve. Together, our 14 
Chapters represent 152,193 dues-paying Sierra Club members within PJM. 
 
We write to you now, almost halfway through a year of change and big questions. Who will pay 
for the costs imposed across the system by new large loads? How will the connection of these 
large loads to the grid affect states' abilities to meet their climate and clean energy goals? As 
you collectively pen your response to the multiple RTO large load policy proposals, as well as 
the pending Notice of Public Rulemaking regarding Large Loads, we write to elevate the 
concerns that 3,972 of our members have shared directly with us. 
 
The Sierra Club has been actively engaged throughout the PJM stakeholder process in the 
development of a regional large load interconnection policy through the Critical Issue Fast Pass 
(CIFP) for Large Load Additions and now via subsequent stakeholder processes (including the 
Backstop Reliability Auction). Yet the gravity of your Public Rulemaking will have broad-reaching 
impacts beyond PJM’s borders.  
 
In Spring 2026, we reached out to our members, many of whom are experiencing the everyday 
burden of increasing electricity bills and are worried about the future of our planet under a world 
of continued fossil extraction that exacerbates the impact of global climate change. These 
members are frustrated that they are being forced to pay the financial and reliability costs that  
hyperscalar data centers and a handful of technology elitists are imposing on a system that is 
not currently equipped to meet this moment of unprecedented growth.  We asked them to share 
their thoughts with you; almost 4,000 people wrote from across PJM and beyond. These 
comments are attached for your review. A number of key principles are woven throughout.  
 
Chiefly, as FERC considers how to address large load additions (LLA) like data centers, your 
decision should be guided by four principles: 
 
 
2101 Webster St. Suite 1300 
Oakland, CA 94612 
 
SierraClub.org 
 

--- PAGE 5 ---
 
 
 
 
 
 
●​ The costs– financial as well as health and other community costs–to power data centers 
should be paid for by technology companies and developers, not residential ratepayers. 
 
●​ State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, 
should not be undermined in the rush to power data centers.​
 
●​ Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and 
geothermal) should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid 
reliability. 
 
●​ Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users, such as data 
centers, at the expense of residential and other consumers, including small consumers, 
and particularly residential ratepayers, who are typically underrepresented in 
decision-making processes. 
 
We need you to make it clear that our power system—which was paid for by everyday people 
across American communities paying their utility bills—serves those customers, not billionaires 
who own technology companies. 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,

APPENDIX B 

--- PAGE 8 ---
To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Will Burke 
Eagle River, AK 99577

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Linda Schilling 
Tempe, AZ 85282

- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Beverly Janowitz-Price 
Phoenix, AZ 85014

underrepresented in decision-making.

our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC):

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Jay Young 
Windsor, CA 95492

- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Derek Dinh 
San Jose, CA 95138

guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Lisa Fields 
Millbrae, CA 94030

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Victoria Shepherd 
Glendale, CA 91201

Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Sarah Hawkinson 
San Diego, CA 92109

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Teresa Johnson 
Colorado Springs, CO 80911

Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities.

- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Lendsay Cape

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities.

guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities:

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Mary Headley 
Longmont, CO 80501

- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Erin Hegarty

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities.

guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential

As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
J Martin 
Henderson, CO 80640

ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Nora Groeneweg

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Harvey Simon 
Washington, DC 20008

AI data centers already make huge negative impact on the citizens. We do not need more of them. 
To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Natalia Shalimo 
Washington, DC 20002

electricity, to cook daily meals, the usage of water because most water pumps and water heaters are 
powered by electricity, and etc.   Electric consumers should not be held accountable for large load 
additions....such an extraordinary will be exceedingly expensive and financially devastating to the 
average consumer. 
To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Regina Williams 
Greenwood, DE 19954

guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Kay Marioni 
Bear, DE 19701

Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities.

guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential

- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
David Kapell 
Hobe Sound, FL 33455

guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Elsie B-W 
Gainesville, FL 32608

Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Lisa Grutzmacher 
Driggs, ID 83422

Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Nancy Brown 
Chicago, IL 60622

- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
vincent vitale 
Glendale Heights, IL 60139

- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Kathryn Podgorski 
Lansing, IL 60438

should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Jake Neff 
Fort Wayne, IN 46809

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Policies to ensure that the lowest-cost energy technologies, including abundant, clean energy like solar, 
wind, battery power, and geothermal come online should be encouraged to match rising electric 
demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should prioritize all consumers, especially small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making, not large industrial users like data centers. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Marilyn Lamm 
Wichita, KS 67203

Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Thomas W Fleitz 
Taylorsville, KY 40071

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability.

should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Tisha Dehart 
Lexington, KY 40517

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Raymond Baugh 
BATON ROUGE, LA 70820

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Beverly Talbot 
Bel Air, MD 21015

As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Marilyn Cekal 
Timonium, MD 21093

should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
karen Christof 
frederick, MD 21703

As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Emma Thomas 
Baltimore, MD 21224

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Beth Nolletti 
Hughesville, MD 20637

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making.

our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Carolyn Morado 
Ann Arbor, MI 48104

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Kathy Hakeem 
Unknown, MI 48886

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Policies to ensure that the lowest-cost energy technologies, including abundant, clean energy like solar, 
wind, battery power, and geothermal come online should be encouraged to match rising electric 
demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should prioritize all consumers, especially small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making, not large industrial users like data centers. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Valerie Smith 
Dimondale, MI 48821

Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Linda Bennett 
Manchester, MO 63021

- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Jessica Dotson 
Cary, NC 27513

Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Carol McWhirter 
Doniphan, NE 68832

Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Cynthia Ortiz 
Hackensack, NJ 07601

electricity cost increases to existing customers, which does not even address the environmental and 
health damages to everyone. 
To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Pat Miller 
Middletown, NJ 07748

should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Liz Depadova 
Morris Plains, NJ 07950

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Lisa Roche 
Lawrence Township, NJ 08648

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Edie Sadowski 
Belleville, NJ 07109

undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

Leslie Lanphear 
Monmouth Junction, NJ 08852

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability.

Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
rob kaminski 
Whiting, NJ 08759

should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires.

Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Beatrice Zovich 
Jersey City, NJ 07304

- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Kenneth Kollinsworth 
Clifton, NJ 07013

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC): 
Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Lisa DiMaulo 
Somerdale, NJ 08083

Artificial intelligence data centers are placing unprecedented new demands on our bulk power system. 
Electric consumers across the country are counting on FERC to work with PJM and other Regional 
Transmission Organizations to ensure grid reliability and affordability in ways that won't compromise 
our environment and communities. 
As FERC considers PJM's proposal for handling large load additions (LLA) like data centers, it should be 
guided by four principles to protect consumers and our communities: 
- The costs to power data centers should be paid for by tech companies and developers, not residential 
ratepayers. 
- Lowest-cost energy technologies (often clean energy like solar, wind, battery power, and geothermal) 
should be encouraged to match rising electric demand and ensure grid reliability. 
- State rights to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be 
undermined in the rush to power data centers. 
- Electric system design should not give preference to larger industrial users like data centers at the 
expense of residential and other consumers, including small residential consumers typically 
underrepresented in decision-making. 
We need FERC and PJM to make it clear that our power grids are meant to serve everyday people and 
our communities, not just Big Tech billionaires. 
Sincerely, 
Hope Hartman 
Wayne, NJ 07470

--- PAGE 1528 ---
